content_list.content_text: When future generations look back on the first decade of the 21st century, they may see it as something of a golden age of European cinema. For it was during this period that European Union incentives, introduced in the 1990s, finally bore fruit: once the material advantages for directors and producers working within Europe had been proven, co-productions stopped being the exception and became the norm.

information.contentText: Following a horror film aesthetic, the film contains extremely violent, highly explicit scenes. Von Trier responded to this in an interview: "I simply thought it would be wrong not to show it. I believe we should put on screen everything we think. I know it is painful to watch, but this film has a lot to do with that pain." The director also stated that he does not believe in God and that this film was a way of passing on to God everything he had learned about Him.

content_list.content_text: Filmmakers such as Michael Haneke (b. 1942) and Paul Verhoeven (b. 1938) can move between different countries - including the United States - without losing their identities as auteurs. Antichrist (2009), by Lars von Trier (b. 1956), was made with European money but shot in English; its leads were a Frenchwoman and an American. However, between that film and Dogville (2003), Von Trier made De Fem Bespaend (The Five Obstructions, 2003) and Direktøren for Det Hele (The Boss of It All, 2006), the two films in his body of work most concerned with Danish issues.

Von Trier is perhaps the greatest example of this malleable form of nationalism and auteur identity. Although he had already made an English-language film in 1996 - Breaking the Waves (1996) - the year 2000 marked the release of his first truly international production, Dancer in the Dark (2000). Starring Björk, the film won two awards at that year's Cannes Film Festival - among them the Palme d'Or. The Swedish film Män Som Hatar Kvinnor (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, 2009), adapted by Niels Arden Oplev (b. 1961) from the novel by fellow Scandinavian Stieg Larsson, proved a hit with both critics and audiences, and an American adaptation was soon planned for 2011.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
information.contentText: The film is based on the 2005 novel of the same name by Swedish writer Stieg Larsson, the first installment of his Millennium series.

content_list.content_text: The two countries that had struggled to find a coherent cinematic identity during the 1980s and 1990s - Germany and Italy - gave rise to two quite distinct, even divergent, movements in the 2000s. From Germany came a series of big-budget films that dealt with historical events without being nostalgic in any way, but were marked by a concern with the country's turbulent past. After directing the modern Das Experiment (The Experiment, 2001), a contemporary look at Nazi psychology, Oliver Hirschbiegel (b. 1957) made, in 2004, Der Untergang (Downfall, 2004), which chronicled the dictator's final days.

quote.quote: A remarkable film that makes you laugh and leaves you thoughtful. It is the work of people with an enormous sense of humor.
quote.author: Philip French on Good Bye, Lenin!

content_list.content_text: The film was followed in 2005 by Sophie Scholl – Die letzten Tage (Sophie Scholl: The Final Days, 2005), a World War II drama directed by Marc Rothemund (b. 1968). In 2003, Wolfgang Becker (b. 1954) took a shrewd look at the aftermath of reunification in the sweetly comic Good Bye, Lenin! (2003), while Uli Edel (b. 1947) turned to the 1970s and the terrorist actions of the Red Army Faction in Der Baader Meinhof Komplex (The Baader Meinhof Complex, 2008).

information.contentText: The film is set during the Battle of Berlin in World War II, when Germany is on the verge of defeat, and depicts the last days of Adolf Hitler (played by Ganz); it is based on the books Der Untergang: Hitler und das Ende des Dritten Reiches, by historian Joachim Fest, and Bis zur letzten Stunde, written by Hitler's former private secretary Traudl Junge, among other accounts by survivors of the period.

content_list.content_text: Yet perhaps it was the Cold War surveillance drama Das Leben der Anderen (The Lives of Others, 2006), directed by Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck (b. 1973), that defined German cinema in the 2000s. The film achieved immense popularity around the world, even winning an Oscar, but it also stirred controversy for its deeply moving and sympathetic portrayal of an officer of the Stasi, the secret police of the German Democratic Republic.

To the defenders of these films, they represented a belated reckoning by the German film industry with the Nazi past. Their detractors, on the other hand, dismissed them as cynical and insensitive attempts to profit from it. The Austrian-German Die Fälscher (The Counterfeiters, 2007), by Stefan Ruzowitzky (b. 1961), attracted considerable attention. Austrian cinema had long been seen as the poor cousin of German cinema, but in the 2000s it was on the rise. Young filmmakers (often women) who came out of the Vienna Film Academy, such as Jessica Hausner (b. 1972), with Lourdes (2009), and Valeska Grisebach (b. 1968), with Sehnsucht (Longing, 2006), produced subtle and original works that sparked international interest.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Lives of Others
information.contentText: The film was released in Germany on March 23, 2006. Around the same time, its screenplay was published by Suhrkamp Verlag. Henckel von Donnersmarck and Ulrich Mühe were sued for defamation over an interview in which Mühe stated that his ex-wife had informed on him to the Stasi during the six years they were married. In the film's publicity material, Henckel von Donnersmarck says that Mühe's ex-wife denied the accusations, despite the existence of 254 pages of official documents from the former East Germany detailing her spying. The film was a success in Germany, despite a widespread reluctance in the country, especially in films, to confront the totalitarian nature of the former East Germany.

content_list.content_text: Italy also looked to the past, but with very different results. Marco Bellocchio (b. 1939) created an unsettling dramatization of the terrorist activities of the 1970s in Buongiorno, notte (Good Morning, Night, 2003). This film, together with Le conseguenze dell'amore (The Consequences of Love, 2004), by Paolo Sorrentino (b. 1970), became a calling card for a new generation of Italian directors, who spoke out both verbally and cinematically against the unbearable weight of the filmic nostalgia that had either stifled the country's cinema or reduced it to a cheap imitation of itself over the previous two decades.

Direct criticism of Silvio Berlusconi's contemporary government was almost impossible, thanks to deplorable acts of censorship. Nevertheless, films such as Mio fratello è figlio unico (My Brother Is an Only Child, 2007) and Gomorra (Gomorrah, 2008) delve into violence and corruption in Italy past and present. These directors' current perspective is marked by new aesthetic approaches that tend to be overstylized, or frenetic and flamboyant, though painted in dull, faded tones - an antidote, perhaps, to the sun-drenched melodramas of the 1980s and the languid pace of the 1960s and of directors such as Michelangelo Antonioni (1921-2007) and Federico Fellini (1920-1993).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Consequences of Love
information.contentText: The film is known for its extremely elegant cinematography. The most memorable scene shows Titta injecting heroin and has the camera rotate 180 degrees as it follows Titta's fall. Brian Gibson of Vue Weekly states that "style becomes substance; cuts and angles create narratives, the surface of the screen opens up depths," pointing to this scene, as well as "gliding cameras, illusions of angle and depth of field [that make] glimpses of human behavior emerge."

content_list.content_text: The United Kingdom, France, and Germany in particular witnessed the emergence of a large number of second- and third-generation directors from ethnic minorities, such as Gurinder Chadha (b. 1960) and Asif Kapadia (b. 1972), Abdellatif Kechiche (b. 1960) and Rachid Bouchareb (b. 1953), Fatih Akin (b. 1973) and Thomas Arslan (b. 1962). Their works deal with issues such as social integration and the way hybrid cultures are negotiated. In Germany, Akin, a Turkish-German filmmaker, set out to change the German perception of a monocultural, ethnically homogeneous society with films such as Gegen die Wand (Head-On, 2004). The Belgian brothers Jean-Pierre (b. 1951) and Luc Dardenne (b. 1954), winners of the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival, were perhaps a classic case of festival filmmakers, 21st-century poetic realists whose bleak reflections on life among the lowest strata of society were acclaimed by critics but failed to draw audiences.

quote.quote: The Lives of Others is one of the few post-reunification films to acknowledge the nightmare of life in communist East Germany.
quote.author: Geoffrey Macnab on The Lives of Others

content_list.content_text: Within what came to be called the new Europe, however, Romania proved to be an exception. Elsewhere, the tendency was for the representation of national cinemas to be limited to a handful of filmmakers who seemed to burst suddenly onto the international circuit, only to fall back into obscurity. Examples include Bosnian Danis Tanovic (b. 1969), with No Man's Land (2001), and Hungarian György Pálfi (b. 1974), with Taxidermia (2006). The early 21st century marked a period of prosperity for European cinema, but the gulf between Eastern and Western Europe remains the same.

movies.overview: A grieving couple retreats to their cabin 'Eden' in the woods, hoping to repair their broken hearts and troubled marriage. But nature takes its course and things go from bad to worse.
movies.title: Antichrist

movies.overview: Titta di Girolamo has been living in a small hotel in Lugano for ten years, he leads a dull and rigid live and has apparently lost his capability to feel human emotion. This all changes when he decides to talk to Sofia, the Barmaid.
movies.title: The Consequences of Love

movies.overview: In April of 1945, Germany stands at the brink of defeat with the Russian Army closing in from the east and the Allied Expeditionary Force attacking from the west. In Berlin, capital of the Third Reich, Adolf Hitler proclaims that Germany will still achieve victory and orders his generals and advisers to fight to the last man. When the end finally does come, and Hitler lies dead by his own hand, what is left of his military must find a way to end the killing that is the Battle of Berlin, and lay down their arms in surrender.
movies.title: Downfall

movies.overview: Selma, a Czech immigrant on the verge of blindness, struggles to make ends meet for herself and her son, who has inherited the same genetic disorder and will suffer the same fate without an expensive operation. When life gets too difficult, Selma learns to cope through her love of musicals, escaping life's troubles - even if just for a moment - by dreaming up little numbers to the rhythmic beats of her surroundings.
movies.title: Dancer in the Dark

movies.overview: An affectionate and refreshing East/West-Germany comedy about a boy whose mother was in a coma while the Berlin wall fell and when she wakes up he must try to keep her from learning what happened (as she was an avid communist supporter) to avoid shocking her which could lead to another heart attack.
movies.title: Good Bye Lenin!

movies.overview: Swedish thriller based on Stieg Larsson's novel about a male journalist and a young female hacker. In the opening of the movie, Mikael Blomkvist, a middle-aged publisher for the magazine Millennium, loses a libel case brought by corrupt Swedish industrialist Hans-Erik Wennerström. Nevertheless, he is hired by Henrik Vanger in order to solve a cold case, the disappearance of Vanger's niece
movies.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo

movies.overview: Head On is German director Fatih Akin’s story of the alcoholic Cahit and Turkish Sibel. Akin tells the story of a love that can never be between two people who are too alike to not be together.
movies.title: Head-On

movies.overview: The story Jewish counterfeiter, Salomon Sorowitsch, coerced into assisting the Nazi operation of the Sachsenhausen concentration camp during World War II.
movies.title: The Counterfeiters

movies.overview: Strange events happen in a small village in the north of Germany during the years just before World War I, which seem to be ritual punishment. The abused and suppressed children of the villagers seem to be at the heart of this mystery.
movies.title: The White Ribbon
movies.original_title: Das weisse Band - Eine deutsche Kindergeschichte

movies.overview: A tragic love story set in East Berlin with the backdrop of an undercover Stasi controlled culture. Stasi captain Wieler is ordered to follow author Dreyman and plunges deeper and deeper into his life until he reaches the threshold of doubting the system.
movies.title: The Lives of Others
